def: Four promises for a transaction: all or nothing, rules kept, no interference from others, and saved even after a crash.
A short reply meaning "got it". Until the sender hears one, it may send the message again.
Many servers around the world share one IP address, and the network sends each user to the nearest one.
One front door in front of your services. It checks who is calling, limits traffic, routes each request and logs it.
A promise that every message arrives, even if that means some arrive twice. So the receiver must cope with repeats.
Adding or removing servers automatically as load changes, based on things like CPU, request rate or queue length.
The sorted, tree-shaped index most SQL databases use. A lookup takes just a few page reads, and changes are made in place.
When a receiver can't keep up, it tells senders to slow down (or some work is dropped) instead of letting it pile up.
A tiny memory-saving check of whether you have seen something. It may say "maybe", but its "no" is always right.
Run two identical copies of your system. Switch all traffic from the old one to the new one, and back if it goes wrong.
Giving each outside service its own separate pool of workers, so one slow service can't use up everyone's share. Like ship compartments.
A small, fast place that keeps the answers you need most, so you rarely go to the slower source.
The share of reads the cache answers without going to the database. Higher means the cache is helping.
The app checks the cache first. If the answer is missing, it asks the database, then saves it in the cache for next time.
Send a small slice of users to the new version first and watch for problems before rolling it out to everyone.
If a network split cuts your copies of the data apart, you can keep answers correct or keep answering, but not both.
Servers around the world that keep copies of your files, so each user downloads from one nearby.
After too many failures, stop calling a broken service for a while and fail right away. Like a fuse in your house.
Storing each column together instead of each row. Reports that need a few columns read less data, and it compresses well.
Update a value only if it still equals what you last saw. If not, it fails, so two writers can't both win.
A set of already-open connections that requests borrow and return, instead of opening a new one every time.
Several machines agreeing on one answer, even when some of them fail or messages get lost.
Servers and keys are placed around a circle. Adding a server moves only about 1/N of the keys, not all of them.
The program that takes messages from a queue or topic and does the work.
A small grid of counters that estimates how often each item appears. It can guess too high, but never too low.
Splitting a system into one part that handles writes and separate parts, shaped for reading, that answer queries.
A data type built so copies can be changed separately, anywhere, and always merge into the same result without conflicts.
Fetching the next page with "give me what comes after this item", not "page 3", so new items don't shift the pages.
A side lookup the database keeps so it can find rows fast, like the index at the back of a book.
A holding area for messages that kept failing after every retry, so people can inspect them and try again later.
Wait until typing pauses before doing the work, so you don't call the search server on every keystroke.
Spotting and dropping repeats, so the same thing is only handled once.
The internet's phone book: it turns a name like example.com into the numeric address of a server.
A money record where every transfer is written twice, as a debit and a credit that cancel out, so balances can always be checked.
How much failure you are allowed: 100% minus your reliability target. You can spend it by shipping risky changes.
Instead of storing the current state, store every change as an event, and rebuild the state by replaying them. Like a bank statement.
Copies may disagree for a moment, but once writes stop they all end up the same.
Throwing items out of a full cache to make room. A policy such as LRU decides which ones go.
A promise that each message is handled once, not twice. In practice it is at-least-once delivery plus ignoring repeats.
Waiting longer after each failed try, such as 1, 2, 4, 8 seconds, so a struggling server gets room to recover.
Switching to a backup when the main machine fails, so the service keeps running.
Copying one event to many places, like a post going to every follower's feed.
When someone posts, copy it into every follower's feed right away, so reading a feed is quick.
A switch in the code you can flip while it runs, to show a feature to some users without deploying again.
A number that goes up with every lock handed out. Storage refuses any holder with an older number, so a stale one can't do damage.
A DNS that gives different answers depending on where the asker is, so users reach a nearby server.
Turns a map position into a short text code. The longer the start two codes share, the closer the places.
Every machine regularly tells a few random others what it knows, so news spreads through the whole cluster fast, like a rumor.
A way to ask one endpoint for exactly the fields you want, in a single request.
A fast way for services to call each other, using compact typed messages (Protobuf) over HTTP/2, with streaming.
A regular "I'm alive" message. If several in a row are missed, the sender is assumed to be down.
Handling more load by adding more machines, instead of buying one bigger machine.
One key that gets far more traffic than the others, so whichever machine holds it is overloaded.
One machine, key or shard that gets far more traffic than the rest, while the others sit idle.
A newer HTTP that sends many requests at once over a single connection and compresses the headers.
The newest HTTP, run over QUIC (which is built on UDP). One lost packet doesn't stall everything, and it connects faster.
Counts roughly how many different items you have seen using only a few kilobytes of memory, with about 1% error.
A unique id sent with a request. On a retry, the server sees the id and returns the saved result.
Safe to repeat: doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. Like pressing an elevator button again.
A list that maps each word to the documents containing it, like a book's index. It powers search.
A little random delay added to waits, so many clients don't all retry at the same moment.
A signed token the server can check without a lookup. Anyone can read it, nobody can forge it, and it's hard to cancel early.
A system that keeps a never-ending ordered log of messages, which many programs can read at their own pace.
Leaving a connection open after a request so the next one skips the setup work.
Two ways to balance load: by network address and port only (L4), or by reading the request itself, like its URL (L7).
A simple counter that orders events by cause and effect, without relying on clocks that may disagree.
How long one request takes, from asking to getting the answer. Like the wait at a shop counter.
Picking one machine to be in charge of writes, usually by majority vote. If it dies, the rest vote for a new one.
Drawing only the rows currently on screen in a long list, and reusing them as you scroll.
How many things are in a system at once equals how fast they arrive times how long each one stays.
A traffic director that spreads incoming requests across several servers, so none gets overloaded.
When overloaded, refuse some requests early so the rest still get a good answer.
The client asks, and the server waits to answer until it has news (or time runs out). Then the client asks again.
An elevator keeps going one way while stops remain ahead, then turns around, so no floor waits forever.
Least recently used: when the cache is full, throw out the item nobody has touched for the longest time.
A storage design for fast writes: save to memory and a log first, flush to sorted files, and merge those files later.
A tree of fingerprints (hashes) where each parent summarizes its children, so two copies find their differences by comparing a few hashes.
A waiting line for messages. One program drops work in, another picks it up later, at its own pace.
Keeping several versions of each row, so readers see a steady snapshot and never block writers.
Databases that give up the strict table-and-join model for flexibility and easier scaling. Cassandra and DynamoDB are examples.
A standard way to let an app use part of your account without ever giving it your password.
A cheap place to keep big files like photos and videos by name, such as S3. Not made for fast tiny lookups.
Don't lock while you work. When saving, check nobody else changed the row (with a version number), and retry if they did.
Save the message to send in the same transaction as the data change. A separate worker sends it later, so a crash can't lose it.
The time that 99 out of 100 requests beat. It shows how slow the unlucky few are, which an average hides.
Extends CAP: during a network split, choose availability or consistency; otherwise, choose between fast answers and consistent ones.
Storing passwords as a deliberately slow, salted scramble (Argon2id, scrypt, bcrypt), never a fast hash like SHA-256.
An extra check for OAuth login in apps that can't keep a secret, like phone or browser apps.
A message that fails every time it is processed, so retrying it never helps.
Asking the server again and again whether anything is new, like checking the mailbox every minute.
The one copy of a database that accepts writes. The replicas copy from it.
A column whose value is unique for every row, so each row can be found directly and never duplicated.
Senders publish messages to a named channel, and everyone subscribed to it gets a copy. The sender doesn't know who listens.
Queries per second: how many requests hit your system each second. A way to size how much load you must handle.
A map split into four squares, then each busy square split into four again, wherever points crowd together.
With N copies, writing to W and reading from R overlap on a fresh copy whenever R + W > N.
A bug where the result depends on which of two actions happens first. Like two people grabbing the last seat.
A way for machines to agree: a majority elects one leader, and a change counts as saved once a majority has it.
Capping how many requests one client can make in a time window, so no one can overwhelm the service.
A copy of the database that answers reads. If the main one fails, it can take over.
A promise that after you save something, you see it when you read, even if the read comes from a copy that is behind.
A very fast database that keeps data in memory. Often used as a cache, a counter store, or a leaderboard.
A copy of a database that follows the main one. It can answer reads and take over if the main one dies.
Keeping copies of the same data on several machines, so you survive a failure and can spread out reads.
How far a replica is behind the main database. During that gap, a read from the replica can return old data.
Moving data between shards when you add or remove machines. It is slow and risky, so pick the key well.
Recovery point objective: the most recent data you can afford to lose in a disaster, measured in time, like the last 5 minutes.
Recovery time objective: how long you can stay down before you must be back up.
A long task split into small steps, each with an "undo" step in case a later one fails. Used instead of one big all-or-nothing transaction.
Sending a query to every shard and merging the answers. It works, but it is only as fast as the slowest shard.
The blueprint of a database: which tables and columns exist, and what kind of value each one holds.
The server keeps one web response open and keeps pushing events to the browser. The browser reconnects by itself if it drops.
How one service finds the live, healthy copies of another, using a registry or DNS.
One slice of a split-up database. Each shard keeps part of the data on its own machine.
The field that decides which shard a row goes to, like user id. A poor choice piles load onto one shard.
Splitting a database into pieces by a key, each on its own machine, so no one machine holds everything.
One part that, if it breaks, takes the whole system down with it.
Layers of linked lists where upper layers let you skip ahead, so search is fast and sorted ranges are easy to scan.
What you measure (SLI), the goal you set (SLO), and the promise you put in a contract (SLA).
A 64-bit id made from the time, a machine number and a counter, so ids come out roughly in time order.
A Redis structure that keeps items ordered by a score. Adding, finding a rank and fetching the top K are all fast.
After a network split, two parts of a cluster each think they are the leader and accept conflicting writes.
The standard language for asking a relational database (tables, rows, joins) for data or changing it.
Many requests find the same cache entry missing at once and all hit the database together.
Each state is its own object that knows how to react to every event, replacing tangled if/else checks on a status field.
A server that remembers nothing between requests, so any copy of it can answer any request.
Sending a user's requests to the same server every time, because that server remembers them.
Handling data continuously as it arrives, with results in seconds instead of waiting for a nightly batch.
A stream processor's guess that all events up to a certain time have arrived, so it can close that time window.
How slow the slowest few requests are, like the slowest 1 in 100. Users feel these even when the average looks fine.
The usual way computers send data reliably: it sets up a connection first and resends anything that gets lost.
TCP delivers data reliably and in order, after a setup handshake. UDP just sends separate packets with no guarantees, but faster.
How much work a system finishes per second. Like cars passing a toll booth each minute.
Lots of clients all acting at the same moment, like retrying or reconnecting together, and swamping a server.
A timer on a stored item. When it runs out, the item is deleted, so stale copies don't stay forever.
The encryption behind https. It scrambles traffic so nobody in between can read or change it.
A rate-limit method: a bucket gets tokens at a steady rate and each request takes one. No token, no request.
A group of database changes that all succeed together or not at all. Like a bank transfer: both sides, or neither.
A coordinator asks everyone "can you commit?" and only if all say yes does it tell them to. If it dies midway, they wait.
A counter per machine attached to every update, so you can tell if one came before another or they happened independently.
Extra points per server on the hash ring, so load spreads more evenly and a failure is shared among many servers.
A web address you give a provider so it calls you when something happens. It may call twice, so ignore repeats by event id.
One connection that stays open, so browser and server can send each other messages at any time.
Two people check the same rule at once, both see it holds, both act, and together they break it.
A log where changes are written to disk before they are confirmed, so after a crash the database can replay them.
Save to the cache right away and write to the database later, in batches. Fast, but a crash can lose recent writes.
Every write goes to the cache and the database together, so the cache is never behind. Writes are a bit slower.
